title: Locke, Berkeley, Hume, and empiricism
note: Empiricists held that all ideas come from experience. Locke called the newborn mind a blank slate; Berkeley concluded that physical things are collections of ideas, sustained by God's perception; Hume traced causation to habit and argued that reason cannot justify inferences from past to future.

read.title: Experience and its limits
text: John Locke argued that there are no innate ideas. The mind begins like blank paper, and every idea comes from sensation of the outer world or reflection on our own mental acts. He distinguished qualities really in bodies, such as shape and motion, from colors and tastes, which are powers in bodies to produce sensations in us.

George Berkeley pushed further. If shape is known only through sensations, as color is, then shape too exists only in being perceived. Talk of matter existing outside every mind is empty. Things are collections of ideas, and their regular order comes from God, who perceives all things and causes our ideas in us.

David Hume asked where our idea of cause comes from. When one billiard ball strikes another, we see only one motion followed by another. After seeing such pairs repeatedly, the mind expects the second event when it sees the first, and this felt expectation is the source of our idea of necessary connection. He also argued that no argument can show the future will resemble the past without assuming it. Hume concluded that such beliefs rest on custom, a natural habit we cannot live without, not on reason.

q.q: Why did Berkeley say shape exists only in being perceived?
o: Shape, like color, is known only through sensation

q.q: According to Hume, what do we actually observe when billiard balls collide?
On what, for Hume, do beliefs about the future rest?
